Concurrent cold calls (and any Dev reload) all proceed to read the manifest and then unconditionally assign entryPointAssetsCache = result, including when result is nil because the read failed. A failing caller can therefore wipe a cache that another goroutine just populated, and return an error even though a valid snapshot already existed. Later non-Dev requests miss the cache and stampede on disk again. Re-read the pointer after Lock and return the existing value when Env is not Dev and the cache is already non-nil; only publish a new pointer on success.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same incomplete double-checked locking bug: GetWebAssets does not re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock, allowing concurrent callers to redundantly populate or overwrite it. The additional consequences and suggested fix do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dual-writer metrics record the wrong store or label

On Storage.Create failure the duration is recorded with recordLegacyDuration (line 45); Storage.Update failure does the same (line 129). Delete success records recordStorageDuration with the object name as the kind label (line 106) instead of options.Kind. DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine records recordStorageDuration (line 166) instead of recordLegacyDuration. true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies Delete success recording metrics with the object name as the kind label instead of options.Kind, which matches the golden issue. The additional metrics issues do not negate this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes are cancelled with the request

Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine using context.WithTimeoutCause on the incoming request context. That child is cancelled as soon as the parent request context is cancelled, which the apiserver does when the handler returns—before the 10s timeout can matter. The legacy write that mode 3 relies on as a safety copy therefore fails with context.Canceled (or never runs to completion), so legacy storage diverges from unified storage while the API still returns success. The goroutines also drop the legacy error instead of logging it, so the failure is silent. Detach from cancellation (for example context.WithoutCancel) before applying the timeout, and log legacy failures.

Legacy update no longer applies the same object snapshot

Update now passes the original objInfo into both Storage.Update and the async Legacy.Update. The previous implementation resolved UpdatedObject once and wrapped that snapshot so both stores wrote the same object. UpdatedObjectInfo is often single-use or not concurrency-safe (patch/apply transformers mutate state and are applied against each store's own current object). Calling it again from the goroutine, concurrently with the in-flight request, can write a different object to legacy, double-apply a patch, or panic. Snapshot the object produced by the unified update and give legacy a fixed UpdatedObjectInfo.

Legacy create receives the object mutated by unified create

After Storage.Create returns, the same obj pointer is passed to the async Legacy.Create. Unified/etcd create fills in resourceVersion, UID, and timestamps on that object. Kubernetes create requires an empty resourceVersion, so the legacy create will be rejected or persist unified-storage metadata. Copy the object before the storage create (or deep-copy the pre-create input for legacy) so the safety write is a real create of the client's object.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy goroutines

Destroy closes Storage and Legacy immediately while Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection may still be running legacy writes in unbounded goroutines. Shutdown or mode switches can destroy a store underneath those calls, dropping the safety write or racing use-after-close. Track the goroutines and wait for them (with the existing timeout) before Destroy returns.

Mode 3 playlist tests assume synchronous legacy writes

The new mode 3 integration cases reuse doPlaylistTests, which immediately lists and gets playlists through the legacy /api/playlists endpoints after k8s create, update, and delete (around the legacy search at line 522 and getFromBothAPIs). Mode 3 returns as soon as unified storage succeeds and only then writes legacy in the background, and that background context is cancelled when the request ends. Those assertions will flake or fail, and they never wait for the legacy write. The unit tests in dualwriter_mode3_test.go have the same gap: they return without waiting for or asserting the legacy mock calls, so a missing or cancelled legacy write still passes.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Spawn flusher processes are never killed or terminated

Processes are created with multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process, but restart and shutdown only call kill()/terminate() when isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process). On Linux the default context Process class is the fork implementation, and SpawnProcess does not subclass it, so the check is false in production. A hung or crashed flusher is therefore left running while _create_process_for_shards starts another daemon on the same shards, and join() never signals the extras to exit. Those overlapping flushers both call flush_segments and produce the same segments to Kafka until the restart cap crashes the consumer, duplicating span data.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. Flusher processes are created with the spawn context, so they are SpawnProcess instances. The isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) check therefore fails on POSIX, and hung processes are never killed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added sleep is a no-op under the time.sleep monkeypatch

test_basic replaces time.sleep with a lambda that returns immediately, then calls time.sleep(0.1) to "give flusher threads time to process" after setting current_drift. That call is the patched function, so it does not wait. The flush still races with join(), which sets stopped immediately, so the test can pass or fail depending on thread scheduling and does not actually cover the timing it was changed to fix.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same problem. time.sleep is monkeypatched, so the added sleep is a no-op and the flusher gets no time to process.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() drops remaining flushers when the deadline hits

join() walks processes and breaks as soon as remaining_time <= 0, before terminate() for that process or any later ones. The previous single-process join always terminated after the wait. With multiple flushers, a timeout therefore leaves later processes running (and, combined with the SpawnProcess isinstance check, never terminates them at all). Shutdown can return while those processes are still flushing and producing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: when the deadline is exceeded, join() breaks out of the loop and skips terminate() for the remaining flusher processes, so they keep running after shutdown.

false_positives.candidate:
Restart does not reap the old flusher before starting the next

After a failed kill(), or even after a successful asynchronous kill()/SIGKILL, the old process object is overwritten without join(). The previous flusher can still be inside flush_segments/produce/done_flush_segments while the replacement process starts on the same shard list and Redis keys. Two flushers then emit the same segments, and unreaped children accumulate as zombies across the up-to-10 restarts.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error timestamps from nodestore are not comparable to breadcrumb timestamps

fetch_error_details copies data.get("timestamp") straight into ErrorEvent. Nodestore event payloads store timestamp as an ISO string, not a float. gen_request_data then compares that value with segment event timestamps using <. A string-vs-number comparison raises TypeError inside the paginator callback and the summarize endpoint returns 500 whenever error context is enabled. Tests only pass because they store a numeric timestamp. The same loop also zips error_ids with events.values(), so a missing nodestore key drops alignment and attaches the wrong title/message/timestamp to an event id.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate's main issue is about timestamp types, but it also explicitly says that zipping error_ids with events.values() loses alignment when a nodestore key is missing, which attaches data to the wrong event id. That matches the golden comment's core concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Table widget flag renders an empty table

When organizations:use-table-widget-visualization is on, tableResultComponent ignores result.data, fields, and metadata and renders TableWidgetVisualization with columns={[]} and tableData.data=[]. Every dashboard table widget becomes blank instead of showing the query result. The flag is a user-visible switch, not a dead code path.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same issue: when the feature flag is enabled, TableWidgetVisualization receives hardcoded empty data and columns, so the table renders empty instead of showing the actual results.

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Assemble analytics runs before auth/feature checks and can 500 the upload

analytics.record(..., user_id=request.user.id) now runs before the organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble feature check and before request body validation. This endpoint is used by org auth tokens (is_org_auth_token_auth later in the handler). If request.user is anonymous or has no id, accessing .id raises and CI assemble uploads fail with 500 even when the feature is enabled and the body is valid. Failures are also recorded as successful assemble events when the feature is off.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate says analytics recording runs before the feature flag check and that events get recorded when the feature is off. That is the same issue as the golden comment, even though the candidate also raises a separate auth concern.

false_positives.candidate:
Merged PR comment helpers are on the wrong class

get_merged_pr_single_issue_template and get_environment_info were added to CommitContextIntegration, but GitHubPRCommentWorkflow and GitlabPRCommentWorkflow call them as self methods. Those workflows subclass PRCommentWorkflow, not CommitContextIntegration, so get_comment_body will raise AttributeError and suspect-issue PR comments will fail. The helper also calls PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title, while _truncate_title is defined only on CommitContextIntegration, so even a direct call would AttributeError.

Hidden span attributes are only removed while searching

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES (is_segment, project_id, received) is applied only inside the searchQuery branch. With an empty search the full attribute list is returned, so those fields stay visible. Typing a query then hides them even when the name matches, which is the opposite of a hide-always filter and makes search results inconsistent with the unfiltered tree.

60s deadline can skip SSO identity refresh for a day

check_auth_identities now has processing_deadline_duration=60 but still refreshes up to chunk_size (100) identities sequentially, each via an external provider call. check_auth already stamps last_synced=now on the whole chunk before this task runs. If the worker hits the 60s deadline mid-chunk, the remaining identities are not refreshed and will not be selected again until the next AUTH_CHECK_INTERVAL (~24h), so SSO validity can stay stale.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).

Account UI message switched to Java MessageFormat

error-invalid-multivalued-size in the account UI bundle was changed from i18next placeholders ({{0}}, {{1}}, {{2}}) to Java MessageFormat ({0}, {1}, {2} plus a {2,choice,...} pattern). Every other string in this file uses {{...}}. The account UI will not substitute the attribute name or limits and will show the literal choice pattern to users when a multivalued attribute fails size validation.

Admin UI messages are interpolated with the {{ }} syntax, not java.text.MessageFormat, so this validation error will render unsubstituted placeholders and the raw choice pattern in the admin console.

Illegal-HTML report can throw and abort the build

When sanitized text differs from the original, the prefix/suffix trim can overlap (for example value "xx" and sanitized "x", or any case where the removed span is made of the same characters as the surrounding text). start + end then exceeds the string length and value.substring / sanitized.substring throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. That RuntimeException is not caught by verify(), so the theme verifier crashes instead of recording the HTML violation.

Lithuanian account TOTP step replaced with Italian

The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Constructor null-check validates grantType twice, not rawTokenId

The fourth requireNonNull call passes grantType again with the message "Null rawTokenId not allowed". A null rawTokenId is therefore accepted and stored. encodeTokenId then concatenates it, producing a jti ending in ":null" (or an NPE later if a caller assumes the id is present). The check must be Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, ...).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug. The fourth requireNonNull checks grantType again instead of rawTokenId, so a null rawTokenId gets past validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Access-token ID matcher rejects valid refresh tokens

isAccessTokenId splits the jti on ':' and then treats items[0].substring(3, 5) as the grant shortcut, returning false when that slice equals the expected shortcut. The encoded prefix is six characters: session type [0,2), token type [2,4), grant type [4,6). substring(3, 5) is therefore the last character of the token type plus the first character of the grant, not the grant shortcut. For a normal refresh access token the prefix is like "onrtrt", so substring(3, 5) is "rt", the condition matches RefreshTokenGrantTypeFactory.GRANT_SHORTCUT, and the matcher returns false. expectRefresh() will fail every regular refresh-token event assertion. The same slice also does not actually check authorization-code, device, or CIBA shortcuts ("onrtac" yields "ta"), so those expectations pass even when the grant shortcut is wrong. Compare items[0].substring(4, 6) and fail when it does not equal the expected shortcut (and when the prefix length is not 6).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug in isAccessTokenId. The candidate says the substring is wrong and should be substring(4,6), which matches the golden comment's first point. It also says the equality check is inverted, since a match currently returns false, which matches the second point.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New getShortcut() breaks existing grant factories and is not length-checked

getShortcut() was added to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory with no default implementation. Every existing custom grant factory fails to compile, and a deployed one throws AbstractMethodError when DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit calls getShortcut(), which aborts server startup. The javadoc also says the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters", but DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId requires the whole context prefix to be exactly 6 characters (2+2+2) and throws IllegalArgumentException otherwise. Nothing in postInit or the hot-deploy refresh path checks that the shortcut is exactly two characters or that it does not collide with another grant after dynamic registration. A 3-character shortcut, which the new contract text encourages, is written into access-token jtis that can never be decoded.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly notes that the javadoc says 'usually like 3-letters' while the implementation requires 2-character shortcuts. That is the same documentation mismatch the golden comment raises, even though the candidate also covers other concerns.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
Federated recovery codes are never consumed and can be replayed

isValid for recovery-authn-codes accepts a submitted code if it equals any value in the stored JSON list and then returns true without removing that code. Combined with getCredentials, which rebuilds the credential via createFromValues from the original full list (all codes unused), a code that has already been used still validates on every later login. Recovery codes are single-use bearer credentials; this storage, which is the implementation the new test relies on, leaves them reusable indefinitely. The new test only logs in once with the first code, so it does not catch the replay.

Successful federated recovery-code login does not retire the credential

After credentialManager().isValid succeeds, the authenticator loads the credential and, when all codes are used, calls removeStoredCredentialById. That API only deletes a credential stored in Keycloak's local credential store. A recovery-code credential created through CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential lives in the user-storage provider when updateCredential returns true, and nothing in this path calls the storage's updateCredential or disableCredentialType to drop or rewrite the used code. The local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider used to mark the code used inside isValid; that provider is skipped once user storage owns the credential. Exhausted or already-used federated codes therefore stay valid, and the required-action fallback never sees allCodesUsed() if the storage returns a freshly rebuilt unused model.

User storage is given every recovery code in plaintext

createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated codes with JsonSerialization and passes that string as the UserCredentialModel challenge response. Local storage stores only hashes (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues / hashRawCode). Any user-storage provider that persists challengeResponse, as the new backwards-compatibility storage does in credentialData, keeps the full set of unused backup codes in cleartext. A compromise of that store exposes codes that can be submitted directly to isValid.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

false_positives.candidate:
Default update-strategy tests never enable rolling-updates

createInitialDeployment returns immediately when updateStrategy is null, before enabling Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES. Both parameterized tests include null (the documented default strategy), and testCacheMaxCount(null) expects a successful rolling update. The new operator guide states that while this is preview the rolling-updates feature must be enabled or the Operator fails. Those cases therefore either fail reconciliation or never exercise the feature the PR says is now required.

Enabling rolling-updates wipes other CR features

When an update strategy is set, the helper replaces the entire enabled-features list with List.of(rolling-updates) instead of appending to any features already on the FeatureSpec. If getTestKeycloakDeployment (or a future caller) has already enabled features, they are dropped on the CR. The server then starts without those features, so upgrade tests can fail or pass for the wrong reason.

Disabled-feature test never checks exit code 4

testFeatureNotEnabled only asserts the stderr text. The contract added in this PR is that metadata/check exit 4 when rolling-updates is disabled (and recreate was moved to 3 so 4 is no longer 'recreate'). Automation is documented to branch on that code. A regression that prints the message but exits 0, 1, or 3 would still pass this test.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
V2 does not clean up permissions when a client is removed

The removal listener now runs only when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is enabled. Under V2, management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 and clients().setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, so the V1 branch cannot be reused, and no V2 branch deletes the authorization resource named by the removed client id. After a client is deleted, orphaned Clients resources and policies remain on the admin-permissions client and can be matched again if that id is reused or shown as dangling permissions.
true_positives.reasoning: Both say the removal listener is guarded only by the V1 flag, so cleanup does not run under V2 and permissions are left orphaned. The candidate focuses on client removal and adds detail about why V1 code can't be reused, but the core issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client id filter includes the type resource name

getClientsWithPermission adds resource.getName() for every Clients-typed resource that grants the scope, including the schema resource whose name is "Clients" rather than a client UUID. Callers that filter the client list by this set will either look up a non-existent client id or, when only an all-clients permission exists, return no clients at all. All-clients access is not expanded to real client ids, so partial-list and query paths that depend on this method are wrong.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. getClientsWithPermission returns the type-level 'Clients' resource name instead of actual client IDs. Callers then look up a non-existent client ID, and real clients are missed.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Per-client resource hides all-clients permissions

hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) loads the resource named by the client id and, if that resource exists, evaluates only that resource. The all-clients resource is consulted only when no per-client resource exists. A client that already has a narrower permission (for example view or configure) will therefore never receive an all-clients manage, view, or map-roles grant, and a negative permission on the type resource will not apply either. Admins who are allowed to manage every client can be forbidden from managing the one client that also has an object-level permission, and the fallback comment in this method is wrong for that case. If getResourceTypeResource returns null, the following findByResource(server, resource) can also NPE instead of denying.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate's main point is a different logic issue, but its last sentence names the same bug: getResourceTypeResource returning null leads to an NPE in findByResource. That matches the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Map-roles checks ignore manage and admin roles

canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission for that one scope. They do not treat AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS or a granted MANAGE permission as sufficient, unlike canManage/canConfigure/canView. With ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 enabled, a realm admin or anyone granted manage-clients (or an all-clients manage permission) is denied mapping client roles, composites, and client-scope roles unless a separate map-roles* permission is also granted. That is an authorization regression versus the V1 evaluator and versus the transitive manage behavior already expected for users.

Existing admin-permissions clients are not migrated

init returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, and nothing else in this change creates the new Clients resource type or the configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite scopes. Realms that already enabled fine-grained admin permissions (Users only) keep the old schema. Creating or evaluating a Clients permission then fails in getOrCreateResource ("No scopes found" / missing type resource) or getScope (scope not in the resource server). Upgraded deployments cannot use the new client permissions without a manual re-init.

Client resource names are not resolved

getResourceName only special-cases the Users type. Client resources created by resolveClient are stored under the internal client id and typically have no display name, so the method falls through to resource.getDisplayName() and returns null. Admin permission APIs and the UI will show a blank name for a client permission instead of the clientId, and a deleted client is not reported as missing the way a missing user is.

requireView javadoc describes a boolean return

The new javadoc on requireView says it returns true if canView() returns true, and requireViewClientScopes is documented the same way. Both methods are void and are specified elsewhere to throw ForbiddenException. Callers reading only these comments will treat a failed check as a boolean result instead of an authorization failure.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
All-groups VIEW permission grants realm-wide group manage

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns true when hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE) succeeds, so an admin who only has the Groups VIEW scope on the all-groups resource is treated as allowed to manage every group. requireManage() is the gate for creating top-level groups (GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup) and other mutations that call canManage() with no group. A view-only fine-grained permission therefore authorizes group creation and other manage operations. canManage() must require MANAGE (or MANAGE_USERS), not VIEW.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: canManage() in GroupPermissionsV2 calls hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE), which lets a user with only VIEW scope pass the manage check. Both say the fix is to require only MANAGE.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Group member search uses authorization resource ids, not group ids

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() walks resources with findByType and then calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId()) and granted.add(groupResource.getId()). In the V2 schema the group id is the resource name (resolveGroup returns group.getId(), and getOrCreateResource stores that as the name); getId() is the authorization resource UUID. hasPermission looks that UUID up with findByName, misses the group resource, and either skips the permission or falls back to the all-groups resource. The set stored on the session as UserModel.GROUPS (UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource searches, and getUsersCount) therefore does not contain group ids. Admins granted view-members or manage-members on specific groups get empty user searches and zero counts, or a filter on ids that match no groups.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses groupResource.getId() (the resource UUID) instead of the resource name (the group id), both for the hasPermission lookup and for the granted set. Both also note the downstream effect on the UserModel.GROUPS filtering and on getUsersCount.

false_positives.candidate:
Per-group authorization resources are created without the Groups type

getOrCreateResource creates a resource named with the group id and updates scopes, but never calls setType(GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE). Only the schema all-groups resource created in init() has type Groups. GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() discovers candidates solely via resourceStore.findByType(..., GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE). Individual group resources are invisible to that scan, so view-members and manage-members permissions on a single group never contribute group ids to user search or user counts. V1 set the type explicitly ("Group"); V2 needs the same when creating the resource.

Existing admin-permissions clients never gain Groups scopes or resources

init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, and this change only adds Groups (and manage-membership, manage-members, view-members) to the schema used at first creation. Realms that already enabled fine-grained admin permissions V2 keep a client with no Groups resource type and no new scopes. Creating a group permission then hits getOrCreateResource, which throws ModelException("No scopes found.") when scopeStore.findByName cannot resolve the new scope names. Permission checks that fall back to getResourceTypeResource also get null and then NPE in GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission on policyStore.findByResource(server, null) or resource.getScopes(). Enabling the feature must migrate an existing admin-permissions client, not only bootstrap a new one.

Group permission resources have no display name

getResourceName() only special-cases the Users resource type and otherwise returns resource.getDisplayName(). Group resources are created with the group id as the name and no display name, and this PR never teaches getResourceName to resolve GROUPS the way it resolves users to usernames. Admin APIs and the UI that list fine-grained permissions will show a null name for every group resource instead of the group name or path.

requireManageMembers javadoc cites the wrong check

The new javadoc on requireManageMembers says it throws if canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false. The method is required to enforce canManageMembers. Callers and implementors following the comment will apply the membership scope instead of manage-members.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider

When this provider is the one selected (standalone authz-client, where no order-200 provider is present), getBouncyCastleProvider() returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the JDK keystore provider (typically SUN), not BouncyCastle. WildFlyElytronProvider returns null for the same method so callers can skip BC registration. Callers that register or look up algorithms on this Provider object will use the wrong JCA provider, so BC-only algorithms and provider-name checks fail or run against SUN instead of failing fast with UnsupportedOperationException like the other unimplemented methods on this class.
true_positives.reasoning: Both say getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider instead of BouncyCastle. Same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementors

order() was added as an abstract interface method with no default. CryptoProvider is a public ServiceLoader SPI. Any out-of-tree or older compiled implementation that is not rebuilt against this change will throw AbstractMethodError as soon as CryptoIntegration.detectProvider calls CryptoProvider::order during startup, and source builds of those providers will fail to compile. A default such as default int order() { return 0; } would keep existing providers loadable while still letting in-repo providers override preference.

false_positives.candidate:
Rebalance shuts down the shared pool, then failed submits are committed

FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy from create_with_partitions. Strategy.close/terminate (and factory.shutdown) call queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts the queues and joins the workers. On the next assignment Arroyo builds a new strategy against that same dead pool. submit() then fails on Queue.put (queue.ShutDown), and the except Exception handler add_offset+complete_offset's the message. The new strategy's commit thread treats that as committable and commits offset+1. Those results are acknowledged and never processed, so uptime checks are dropped after the first revoke/rebalance or any close().

Queues are unbounded, so submit never applies backpressure

Each work queue is queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and FixedQueuePool.submit always put()s without blocking. The class docstring claims natural backpressure when queues fill, but the Arroyo consumer thread can keep polling and enqueueing forever while workers lag. A slow subscription (the case this mode is meant to isolate) or a dead worker grows memory without bound and can OOM the process. submit() needs a bounded queue and must block (or otherwise stall the consumer) when that queue is full.

Offsets are committed from a background thread

_commit_loop runs on a daemon thread started in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy and calls the Arroyo commit callback directly. That callback commits through the Kafka consumer, which the processor is also using on the main thread for poll, assignment, and close. librdkafka consumers are not thread-safe; concurrent commit and poll/close can crash the consumer or corrupt the group offset. Commits need to be handed back to the processing thread (for example recorded in poll() and committed there).

Shutdown joins every worker for 5s and join() drops the timeout

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown then queue.shutdown, then joins each worker with timeout=5.0 in series. A worker blocked in result_processor (DB/HTTP) does not notice shutdown until the current item finishes, so N queues can block shutdown for about N*5 seconds (100s at the default 20). SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join ignores the timeout Arroyo passes and always calls close(), which also joins the commit thread for another 5s before shutting the pool. A revoke or process shutdown can therefore exceed the Kafka session/max.poll interval and trigger another rebalance while workers are still running. join() must honor its timeout, and worker joins need a single shared deadline.

Graceful shutdown does not drain queued work before stopping commits

OrderedQueueWorker.run checks self.shutdown at the top of the loop, and FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets that flag before waking the workers. A worker that finishes the current item, or that is unblocked from get() with items still queued, exits without processing the rest of the queue. close() also stops and joins the commit thread before pool.shutdown(), so anything completed after the last commit iteration is never committed by this strategy, and anything still queued is abandoned. Arroyo's join contract is that submitted messages are finished or the timeout fires; here in-flight uptime results are dropped on the floor until a later replay, and a replay will not happen for any offset the commit thread already advanced past.

Queue stats test can pass or fail depending on worker timing

test_stats_reporting submits 10 items and immediately asserts get_stats()['total_items'] > 0. Workers are already running, so a fast result_processor can drain every queue before that assertion. The same file's test_different_groups_distributed asserts that 20 hashed keys always land on all 3 queues, which hash() does not guarantee. Both tests will flake under load or a different PYTHONHASHSEED.

The cache key is error_upsampling_eligible:{org}:{hash(sorted project ids)} with a 60s TTL. hash() is salted per process for non-int values, and even for ints it is not a stable cross-version key; workers will miss or collide, so the stated cross-request cache does not work. invalidate_upsampling_cache builds the same key but is never called when issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist changes, so a stale True remains for up to 60s and keeps rewriting count() after a project is removed from the allowlist (and a stale False keeps serving un-upsampled counts after it is added). Integration tests patch options.get but do not clear this cache, so a reused project id can make the allowlist tests assert the wrong count.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly points out that hash() is salted per process, so cache keys won't match across workers. This is the same issue as the golden comment. The candidate adds further concerns, but the core issue is present.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision uses the outer dataset, not the dataset that runs

is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects is called with the endpoint's outer dataset, while _get_event_stats runs scoped_dataset, which dashboard widget splitting can change to discover or back to the metrics dataset. _should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns true for the errors module unconditionally and false for transactions. If the outer dataset is errors but the executed dataset is discover/transactions (or the reverse), count() is rewritten, or not rewritten, for the wrong dataset. Transaction queries can then reference sample_weight, and error queries can keep a raw count() and under-report volume.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: the upsampling check is passed the outer dataset rather than scoped_dataset, so dashboard split paths make the wrong upsampling decision. The candidate's examples differ somewhat from the golden's, but the underlying issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Error detection is a substring check on the original request, not the executed query

_is_error_focused_query returns true when the raw request.GET query string contains the substring event.type:error. That matches negated filters such as !event.type:error, so a discover query that explicitly excludes errors is still rewritten from count() to upsampled_count()/sum(sample_weight). The check also ignores the query string actually executed: _get_event_stats passes the closed-over request into is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects, not the query argument. Dashboard discover-split builds transactions_only_query / errors_only_query and still calls _get_event_stats with the original request, so a request whose query contains event.type:error will upsample the transaction-only split query (sample_weight is not valid for transactions), and an errors-only split of a query that does not contain that substring will not upsample. Counts will be wrong or the Snuba query will fail.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key collides when UIDs contain underscores

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates action, name, and parent with "_" and no delimiter that cannot appear in a UID. Grafana short UIDs may contain underscores, so name "foo" + parent "bar_baz" and name "foo_bar" + parent "baz" produce the same key. A cached deny for one resource then makes Check return Allowed=false for a different resource the user is allowed to access, for the full denial TTL.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem: userPermDenialCacheKey builds keys by joining components with underscores, so components that contain underscores can produce colliding keys and wrong denial cache hits. The candidate gives a concrete example of such a collision.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache blocks the DB requery this PR adds

Check consults permDenialCache before cached permissions or the database, and on any final deny it stores that key for shortCacheTTL (30s). A later grant never clears the entry, so the new "requery when the scope is missing from cached permissions" path is skipped and Check keeps returning Allowed=false. That is the creator flow this PR is meant to fix: a check before the dashboard/folder permission row exists (or before a just-created parent is in the folder tree) records a deny, and the follow-up open still fails until the denial entry expires even if getIdentityPermissions would now allow it. Revocation stays cached on the allow path, so denials are strictly stickier than grants.

List still serves stale permission cache

List returns getCachedIdentityPermissions immediately on a cache hit and never requeries when a newly created dashboard or folder scope is absent. Check was changed to fall through to the DB in that case, so after creation Check can allow a resource that List still omits for up to shortCacheTTL (30s). Callers that "fetch" newly created dashboards/folders via List keep the bug this PR describes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reinstall crashes when metadata has no sender

After an Integration exists with no OrganizationIntegration, the code always evaluates integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]. build_integration only stores sender when pipeline state already has it, and this pipeline never binds sender, so installs created through the pipeline (and any older rows whose webhook payload did not write metadata.sender) have no sender. Re-attaching those installations raises KeyError instead of the integration error page, so a previously working reinstall 500s and never reaches next_step.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe a KeyError from accessing integration.metadata['sender']['login'] without checking that the sender key exists, which breaks integrations created without sender metadata.

false_positives.candidate:
Installer identity is not checked on first link

The new GitHub-user check only runs after an Integration row already exists and has no OrganizationIntegration. If Integration.DoesNotExist, dispatch returns pipeline.next_step() immediately and build_integration links that installation_id to the current Sentry org with no comparison to github_authenticated_user. GitHub fires the installation webhook and the browser redirect in parallel, so an attacker who knows a victim installation_id can finish this pipeline before the webhook creates the Integration, attach the victim's GitHub App install to the attacker's org, and then block the real installer via the "already installed on another organization" path. The OAuth step therefore does not enforce the mismatch failure described in the PR for the claim-on-create path.

User-mismatch test cannot tell a state failure from the new check

test_github_user_mismatch (and the rewritten test_installation_not_found) only assert the generic "Invalid installation request." body. That same string is returned for a state/signature mismatch, a bad OAuth code, a missing login, and the sender comparison. The mismatch test also reuses the hardcoded state 9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3 after login_as(user_2) and a new org pipeline, so a state mismatch fails the request before GitHubInstallation ever compares logins. Nothing asserts that a matching installer is allowed, that a missing Integration is rejected, or that the 404 installation path still surfaces, so the security control can be bypassed or broken without these tests failing.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

testCacheIDPForLogin registers cleanup with testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove (same mistake again at the hide-on-login IdP around line 425). The providers are created as idp-alias-0 … idp-alias-20, so this resource does not refer to them and they are left in the shared test realm. A second run, or any later test that counts realm or login IdPs, will see the leaked brokers and the exact size assertions (5, 6, 10, 11) will fail.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation uses org-wrapped isEnabled()

update() passes the model from getById() into registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(). With organizations enabled, getById() returns an anonymous IdentityProviderModel whose isEnabled() is false when the organization is missing, disabled, or the organization provider is off, even if the stored IdP is enabled. LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate() calls that override. If the organization is disabled, an IdP that is already in the getForLogin cache looks ineligible, and an update that also fails the predicate for a real reason (hideOnLogin, linkOnly, or kc.org.broker.public set to false) hits the early return and does not invalidate .idp.login.*. After the organization is enabled again, getForLogin still returns that IdP and the login page can show a link-only or non-public organization broker. false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL kill switch inverts the flag and always returns false

enableSqlExpressions sets enabled to the negation of FlagSqlExpressions and then returns false from both branches, so the flag is never honored and the control flow does not match the function name. This is the only gate on the ExpressionQueryReader SQL path (the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented" at the call site). A reviewer "correcting" the obvious inversion so the fall-through returns true would turn SQL expressions back on whenever the documented feature flag is enabled, which is exactly the CVE-2024-9264 surface. The disablement should be an explicit return false with a comment that SQL expressions are hard-disabled because of that CVE, and it should not read the flag with a negated condition.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same function and the same flaw: the flag is negated and both branches return false, so SQL expressions are always disabled. The candidate adds CVE context, but the core issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Disabled SQL expressions report "not implemented"

When a SQL expression is rejected, ReadQuery returns fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented"). The feature was implemented and is being turned off to stop RCE/LFI (CVE-2024-9264); the feature flag and its docs are intentionally left in place. Operators who enable that flag, or clients that already send type=sql, will treat this as a missing feature or a bad deploy rather than a security disablement, and may try to turn the flag on or restore DuckDB. The error should say SQL expressions are disabled.

No test that SQL expressions cannot reach DuckDB

The CVE fix removes go-duck and stubs DB.RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList, and rejects QueryTypeSQL in ExpressionQueryReader. Nothing in the change asserts either entry point. UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand still calls sql.TablesList, which still interpolates the user query into SELECT json_serialize_sql('...') and only fails because the stub returns an error; Execute still calls QueryFramesInto. A regression that restores a real in-memory DB, or that drops the reader check, would not be caught. Add a test that both ReadQuery and UnmarshalSQLCommand/Execute reject SQL expressions and never invoke a real engine.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache fill is not rechecked under the write lock

GetWebAssets drops the read lock and then takes the write lock without checking entryPointAssetsCache again. Concurrent cold calls (and any Dev reload) all proceed to read the manifest and then unconditionally assign entryPointAssetsCache = result, including when result is nil because the read failed. A failing caller can therefore wipe a cache that another goroutine just populated, and return an error even though a valid snapshot already existed. Later non-Dev requests miss the cache and stampede on disk again. Re-read the pointer after Lock and return the existing value when Env is not Dev and the cache is already non-nil; only publish a new pointer on success.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same problem: after acquiring the write lock, GetWebAssets does not re-check the cache. This is the missing second check in the double-checked locking pattern.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache fill is not rechecked under the write lock

Concurrent cold calls (and any Dev reload) all proceed to read the manifest and then unconditionally assign entryPointAssetsCache = result, including when result is nil because the read failed. A failing caller can therefore wipe a cache that another goroutine just populated, and return an error even though a valid snapshot already existed. Later non-Dev requests miss the cache and stampede on disk again. Re-read the pointer after Lock and return the existing value when Env is not Dev and the cache is already non-nil; only publish a new pointer on success.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says the cache is unconditionally assigned even when result is nil because the read failed, which wipes a valid cache. It also suggests publishing a new pointer only on success. This is the same issue as the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup logs full ID batches at Error level

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error on every batch for both the ID fetch and the delete (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including the full ids slice and the SQL condition. These run on the success path (err is nil) and again when a batch finds nothing. With AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize in the thousands, each line can dump tens of thousands of IDs. That floods production logs, trips error-based alerts, and allocates large log payloads on every cleanup cycle. These should be removed or dropped to debug without the ID list before merge.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag Error-level logging used for debug/success-path information that pollutes production logs, and both recommend switching to debug. The candidate adds detail about large ID payloads, but the core issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker shortened from 10 minutes to 1 minute

Run now uses time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1) instead of 10 minutes. The PR is only about splitting annotation cleanup queries to avoid MySQL deadlocks; nothing in the description changes the job cadence. clean() still uses a 9-minute timeout that was sized for a 10-minute period, so a slow cycle now finishes and immediately starts another. Annotation cleanup is exactly the workload that was deadlocking writers, so running it about 10x more often increases DB load and makes that failure mode more likely. Restore the 10-minute interval unless the schedule change is intentional and the timeout is updated to match.
true_positives.reasoning: Both flag the cleanup ticker being cut from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which raises DB load and contention. The candidate covers the same concern and adds more detail.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation

When the dialect is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is above 999, deleteByIDs builds the IN-list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) once per ID. Each iteration copies the entire growing string. The new test uses batch size 32767, so this path copies on the order of hundreds of megabytes to gigabytes of intermediate strings per DELETE and can stall or time out cleanup (and CI) for a batch that was supposed to be a simple workaround for SQLite's parameter limit. Build the list with strings.Builder or strings.Join instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dual-writer metrics record the wrong store or label

On Storage.Create failure the duration is recorded with recordLegacyDuration (line 45); Storage.Update failure does the same (line 129). Delete success records recordStorageDuration with the object name as the kind label (line 106) instead of options.Kind. DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine records recordStorageDuration (line 166) instead of recordLegacyDuration. Failure and latency dashboards for mode 3 will attribute unified-storage errors to legacy, legacy delete-collection latency to storage, and delete metrics to a per-object series, so the safety-write signal this mode depends on is wrong.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says Delete records metrics with the object name as the kind label instead of options.Kind. That is the same issue as the golden comment. The candidate also raises other problems, but this one matches.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes are cancelled with the request

Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine using context.WithTimeoutCause on the incoming request context. That child is cancelled as soon as the parent request context is cancelled, which the apiserver does when the handler returns—before the 10s timeout can matter. The legacy write that mode 3 relies on as a safety copy therefore fails with context.Canceled (or never runs to completion), so legacy storage diverges from unified storage while the API still returns success. The goroutines also drop the legacy error instead of logging it, so the failure is silent. Detach from cancellation (for example context.WithoutCancel) before applying the timeout, and log legacy failures.

Legacy update no longer applies the same object snapshot

Update now passes the original objInfo into both Storage.Update and the async Legacy.Update. The previous implementation resolved UpdatedObject once and wrapped that snapshot so both stores wrote the same object. UpdatedObjectInfo is often single-use or not concurrency-safe (patch/apply transformers mutate state and are applied against each store's own current object). Calling it again from the goroutine, concurrently with the in-flight request, can write a different object to legacy, double-apply a patch, or panic. Snapshot the object produced by the unified update and give legacy a fixed UpdatedObjectInfo.

Legacy create receives the object mutated by unified create

After Storage.Create returns, the same obj pointer is passed to the async Legacy.Create. Unified/etcd create fills in resourceVersion, UID, and timestamps on that object. Kubernetes create requires an empty resourceVersion, so the legacy create will be rejected or persist unified-storage metadata. Copy the object before the storage create (or deep-copy the pre-create input for legacy) so the safety write is a real create of the client's object.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy goroutines

Destroy closes Storage and Legacy immediately while Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection may still be running legacy writes in unbounded goroutines. Shutdown or mode switches can destroy a store underneath those calls, dropping the safety write or racing use-after-close. Track the goroutines and wait for them (with the existing timeout) before Destroy returns.

Mode 3 playlist tests assume synchronous legacy writes

The new mode 3 integration cases reuse doPlaylistTests, which immediately lists and gets playlists through the legacy /api/playlists endpoints after k8s create, update, and delete (around the legacy search at line 522 and getFromBothAPIs). Mode 3 returns as soon as unified storage succeeds and only then writes legacy in the background, and that background context is cancelled when the request ends. Those assertions will flake or fail, and they never wait for the legacy write. The unit tests in dualwriter_mode3_test.go have the same gap: they return without waiting for or asserting the legacy mock calls, so a missing or cancelled legacy write still passes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Filtered Grafana rules are rendered without a list key

The grafana branch of the filtered-results map used to pass key={key} into GrafanaRuleLoader. The replacement GrafanaRuleListItem element has no key, while the datasource and unknown branches still do. React will reuse the wrong row when the filter result set grows or shifts, so rule names, health, and action buttons can attach to the wrong rule. getRuleKey already exists for this list specifically to avoid duplicate keys.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say the GrafanaRuleListItem rendered in the list has no React key prop, which can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.

Silence menu item does not open the drawer

AlertRuleMenu can show Silence notifications from Grafana Prometheus abilities and calls handleSilence, which only sets showSilenceDrawer. The drawer itself is still gated on rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) and is passed rulerRule. In the list view rule is undefined, so clicking Silence does nothing. false_positives.candidate:
Delete never appears in the ruler-free list view

canDelete is now true when Grafana Prometheus abilities allow delete, but the Delete menu item is still rendered only when rulerRule is set, and its click handler still requires that ruler DTO. GrafanaRuleListItem (the new list view) passes only promRule, so the item is never shown even for users with folder delete permission. The new GrafanaGroupLoader test grants AlertingRuleDelete and then asserts the menu has exactly four items and does not include Delete, so this regression is untested. The list view no longer loads ruler rules and only supplies promRule, so the pause item is never rendered even though useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities can set canPause. Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable

useAllAlertRuleAbilities used to set isFederated from isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group), which blocked update, delete, pause, restore, and permanent delete. After this refactor it always delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated to false (the source_tenants check is commented out and RuleGroupIdentifierV2 is not used to recover it). The removed GrafanaRuleListItem built the view href with createReturnTo() so Back returned to the filtered or grouped list. The new item calls createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`) with no returnTo query. $__range queries are interpolated before the no-split guard

runSplitQuery now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables on every target before querySupportsSplitting(). That helper intentionally refuses to split expressions containing $__range / $__range_ms / $__range_s because those macros must be interpolated against each chunk's time range (the comment at the guard says the backend does that with the split range). After this change the macro is replaced using the original full request range, so isQueryWithRangeVariable() no longer matches and the query is time-split anyway. Each chunk then runs with a range duration for the whole query, producing wrong rates/counts (and the same path is hit again from runShardSplitQuery, which interpolates before delegating to runSplitQuery). The new tests only cover $__auto and $step, so this regression is untested. Preserve the range-variable check on the pre-interpolation expression and do not split those queries.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check and insert are not atomic

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts recent devices and, if the count is under AnonymousDeviceLimit, inserts in a separate session with no transaction or row lock. Concurrent first-time devices can all observe count < limit and all insert, so the stored device count exceeds the configured cap and anonymous auth is granted past the limit. The count and the insert/upsert need to be serialized (single transaction with a lock, or an insert that fails when the cap is already reached).
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race condition: concurrent requests pass the device count check before inserting, so the device limit is exceeded. Both also suggest a transaction or lock as the fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is set before the limit check, so a rejected device is allowed on retry

tagDeviceUI writes the device cache key before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, Authenticate fails once, but the key stays cached for 29 minutes. The next request for that device hits the cache, TagDevice returns nil, and anonymous authentication succeeds without ever recording the device. The configurable limit is therefore bypassed by any client that retries within the cache TTL. Set the cache only after a successful write, and do not treat a cached rejection as success.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug. The cache is set before CreateOrUpdateDevice, so after ErrDeviceLimitReached the cached entry remains for 29 minutes, and later requests bypass the device limit.

false_positives.candidate:
Wire providers changed but generated injectors are not updated

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService no longer takes anonstore.AnonStore and now takes db.DB, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained an int64 deviceLimit argument. Grafana builds this graph with Google Wire and commits wire_gen.go; this PR does not update wire.go or wire_gen.go. Wire cannot provide a bare int64 to ProvideAnonDBStore, so regeneration will fail and the current generated injector will not compile against the new signatures.

device_limit is not added to defaults.ini

auth.anonymous device_limit is read via MustInt64(0) (0 means unlimited) but conf/defaults.ini and sample config are unchanged. Operators have no documented key, default, or meaning, and Grafana config docs are generated from defaults.ini, so the new limit cannot be discovered or set from the shipped configuration.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locale files are not loaded on translate

The on-demand loader in I18n.translate only calls load_locale for config.locale. FallbackLocaleList and I18n::Backend::Fallbacks then look up SiteSetting.default_locale and :en, but those YAML files stay unloaded unless something else has called ensure_loaded!. The only call site is ApplicationController#set_locale, so jobs, mailers, models, middleware, and I18n.with_locale blocks never load the fallback chain. Missing keys then raise or return the Rails "translation missing" string instead of the site-locale or English string. Because translate also LRU-caches that result (and the production exception handler returns a string rather than raising), a miss can stick in the cache even after the fallback files are loaded later in the same process.

The importer used to create the topic from the XML export. It now calls `TopicEmbed.import_remote`, which `open`s `t[:link]` with no rescue. true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same problem as the golden comment. On the animated GIF path, gifsicle's --resize-fit expects WxH geometry, so passing "80%" makes downsizing fail silently.

The upload Tempfile is already open, so a convert that writes via a new inode leaves that FD on the original bytes while `tempfile.size` and `Upload.create_for` still use the open file. The candidate's main point is that using the same path for input and output corrupts the file. It does also say the open FD keeps the original bytes, so tempfile.size reports stale data and downsizing no-ops. A second GET then takes the else branch and mutes them, so refresh or a double click changes the level again.

The only test change passes unsubscribe_url into MessageBuilder and still only asserts that the preferences URL appears. Nothing covers TopicsController#unsubscribe: missing TopicUser, watching vs regular vs muted outcomes, notifications_reason_id being set, idempotent repeats, or the email string interpolating unsubscribe_url. true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:

A zero-length date override (start equal to end) is the usual way an organizer marks a day unavailable. The check compares two separately constructed dayjs objects with ===, which is reference equality and is always false, so that branch never runs. Combined with the early return when dateOverrideExist is set, a blocked day is treated as fully available instead of closed, and busy times on that day are also skipped.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point out that the code compares two dayjs objects with ===, which checks reference equality and is therefore always false. The candidate adds the consequences: zero-length overrides never match, so blocked days are treated as available. The underlying bug is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Override days skip busy checks and can double-book

In checkIfIsAvailable, once any date override falls on the same calendar day as the slot, dateOverrideExist is set and the function returns true as soon as the slot is not rejected as outside that override. That return happens before the busy-interval loop. Fixed hosts and round-robin hosts therefore look free for every slot inside an override window even when they already have a Cal booking or calendar conflict covering that time, so the booking page will offer times that cannot actually be taken.

slotStartTime is a UTC dayjs, but the override side is dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset).format(...), which formats in the server's local timezone, not UTC or the organizer zone. The offset itself is also applied to an absolute instant and then compared with UTC slot instants. On any host whose TZ is not UTC, or when the organizer offset moves the override across midnight, the same-day test and the isBefore/isAfter window checks attach the override to the wrong day or the wrong clock times, so fixed-host overrides still do not constrain the slots the PR is trying to fix.

Override start and end are shifted by inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset and then reduced to hour() and minute() only. If the shift crosses midnight, hour() wraps to the other side of the day (for example 01:00 minus a 10h offset becomes 15:00) and the previous/next day is discarded. buildSlots then places that window on the invitee's current day. Attendees in a timezone far from the organizer see the override on the wrong date, or miss it, which is the timezone bug this change is meant to fix whenever the adjusted range is not on the same calendar day.

New test does not cover either bug the PR claims to fix

The only added assertion re-requests the same personal-event override in Asia/Dhaka and expects the identical UTC slot list. It never builds a round-robin event with a fixed host, never asserts that slots outside the fixed host's override disappear, and never checks that an override moves to a different invitee-local calendar day. A regression in checkIfIsAvailable or in the midnight-crossing offset math would still pass CI.

The retryCount > 1 OR branch lacks a method: SMS filter, so it deletes EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders even though the job should only remove SMS reminders. A wrong OR (as written) silently drops live reminders and would not be caught before merge.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reschedule calendar/video cleanup is not awaited

getCalendar is now async, but the only call site wraps it in bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...). forEach does not wait for async callbacks, and the returned promises are discarded, so the try/catch around it never sees rejections from getCalendar or deleteEvent/deleteMeeting. Reschedule then sends the reschedule email and returns true while external calendar events and video meetings may still be deleting, or may fail as unhandled rejections and leave the old event on the calendar.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: forEach is used with async callbacks for calendar/video deletions, so the promises are never awaited. That causes unhandled rejections, a try/catch that catches nothing, and incomplete cleanup.

false_positives.candidate:
Wipe-my-cal reschedule cleanup is not awaited

Same as the vital reschedule path: bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...) awaits getCalendar only inside a callback that nothing awaits. Calendar deleteEvent and video deleteMeeting are not part of the function's control flow, the surrounding try/catch cannot handle their failures, and the handler can finish (and email the user) before those integrations are actually torn down.

requestReschedule does not wait for integration deletes

requestReschedule now awaits getCalendar inside bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...), which does not await the callback. deleteEvent/deleteMeeting promises are dropped, so the mutation proceeds to send the reschedule email and BOOKING_CANCELLED webhooks without knowing whether the old calendar event or video meeting was removed. Failures become unhandled rejections instead of failing the mutation.

Cancel-all recurring events never waits on calendar deletes

When cancelling all remaining instances of a recurring booking, credentials are walked with .forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent) }). The callback is not awaited, and deletedEvent is the resolved value, not a promise, pushed only after deleteEvent finishes. Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)) later in the handler therefore runs before those pushes, so recurring calendar events are not reliably deleted and errors are not surfaced to the cancel request. The non-recurring branch just below was correctly converted to for...of; this branch was not.

Dynamic imports still load every app immediately

Each app is stored as import("./...") in an object literal, so every promise starts as soon as this module is evaluated. Any importer of appStore (calendar, video, payment, bookings) therefore kicks off a load of every integration at once. That does not defer unused apps, and it replaces one static graph with many parallel chunks that all start together, which can make cold starts slower rather than lazy.
